content: The clinical management of intermittent exotropia (X(T)) has been widely studied, but there is still no consensus on when to intervene, which treatment is most effective, or the optimal timing for treatment during the progression of the condition. This review aimed to evaluate the effects of various surgical and non-surgical treatments in randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving individuals with intermittent exotropia. It also sought to identify criteria for intervention and assess whether treatment outcomes differ based on age or subtype of X(T). The search for relevant studies was conducted using multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid Embase, LILACS, the ISRCTN registry, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO ICTRP. The search was completed on January 20, 2021. Additional manual searches were performed in the British Orthoptic Journal (up to 2002) and the proceedings of the European Strabismological Association (ESA), International Strabismological Association (ISA), and American Association for Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus (AAPOS) meetings (up to 2001). The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluated any surgical or non-surgical treatment for intermittent exotropia. Standard Cochrane methodology was followed for data collection and analysis. Six RCTs were included in the review, with four conducted in the United States and two in Asia (Turkey and India). A total of 890 participants with basic or distance X(T) were included, most of whom were children aged 12 months to 10 years. Three of the six studies were carried over from the 2013 version of this review. The included studies had a high risk of performance bias because it was not possible to mask participants and personnel administering the treatments. Two RCTs compared bilateral lateral rectus recession with unilateral lateral rectus recession combined with medial rectus resection. However, only one RCT (n = 197) reported on the primary outcomes of the review. Bilateral lateral rectus recession likely results in minimal differences in motor alignment at near fixation (mean difference [MD] 1.00, 95% confidence interval [CI] −2.69 to 4.69) and distance fixation (MD 2.00, 95% CI −1.22 to 5.22) as measured by the prism and alternate cover test (PACT). This evidence was of moderate certainty. Bilateral lateral rectus recession may also result in little to no difference in stereoacuity at near fixation (risk ratio [RR] 0.77, 95% CI 0.35 to 1.71), adverse events (RR 7.36, 95% CI 0.39 to 140.65), or quality of life measures. These findings were supported by low-certainty evidence. A meta-analysis of two RCTs compared patching (n = 249) with active observation (n = 252). Patching was found to be clinically more effective than active observation in improving motor alignment at near fixation (MD −2.23, 95% CI −4.02 to −0.44) and distance fixation (MD −2.00, 95% CI −3.40 to −0.61) as measured by PACT at six months. This evidence was of high certainty. However, patching resulted in little to no difference in stereoacuity at near fixation (MD 0.00, 95% CI −0.07 to 0.07), based on low-certainty evidence. Stereoacuity at distance, motor fusion test results, and quality of life measures were not reported. Adverse events were also not reported, but the study authors noted that adverse events were not expected due to the non-surgical nature of patching. One RCT (n = 38) compared the prism adaptation test followed by eye muscle surgery with eye muscle surgery alone. However, no review outcomes were reported for this comparison. Another RCT (n = 60) compared lateral rectus recession combined with medial rectus plication versus lateral rectus recession combined with medial rectus resection. The evidence suggested that lateral rectus recession with medial rectus plication may not improve motor alignment at distance fixation (MD 0.66, 95% CI −1.06 to 2.38), based on low-certainty evidence. The effect of this intervention on motor fusion test performance was very uncertain (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.48 to 1.74), based on very low-certainty evidence. In conclusion, patching provides a clinical benefit for children aged 12 months to 10 years with basic or distance-type intermittent exotropia compared to active observation. However, there is insufficient evidence to determine whether other interventions, such as bilateral lateral rectus recession versus unilateral lateral rectus recession with medial rectus resection, lateral rectus recession with medial rectus plication versus lateral rectus recession with medial rectus resection, or prism adaptation test prior to eye muscle surgery versus eye muscle surgery alone, offer any significant benefit.
